Received 15 October 2024 l Revised 14 January 2025 l Accepted 26 January 2025 l Published online 28 May 2025 Abstract: Objective: This study aimed to determine the antioxidant, antibacterial, and anti-inflammatory activities of ethanol extracts from red Dadap flowers (Erythrina crista-galli L). In addition to formulate the extract into a moisturizing gel preparation of good physical quality. Material and Methods: Antioxidant activity was determined using a 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radical scavenging capacity assay. Antibacterial activity was evaluated using the disc diffusion method. Anti-inflammatory activity was evaluated using carrageenan-induced paw edema in mice in vivo. Additionally, in silico studies were performed and the physical quality of the extract-gel formulation was evaluated. Results: Antioxidant testing resulted in a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC ) value of 79.1 ppm and an AAI 50 value of 0.4. Antibacterial testing obtained the largest inhibition zone, with an average of 9.0 mm. Anti-inflammatory testing obtained the greatest anti-inflammatory effect at a dose of 300 mg/kg body weight in mice, with a percentage of inflammation inhibition that reached 59.32%. In silico testing, the smallest binding affinity values were obtained: respectively, at -10.3, -12.0, and -10.2 kcal/mol, by the specific compound Cyanidin-3-O-glucoside. Physical quality evaluation obtained values that are in accordance with the Indonesian National Standard. Contact: Chaerul Fadly Mochtar, B.Pharm., M.Biomed. JSON: Name: erythrina_gel_bioactivity_pipeline Title: Integrated in vitro, in vivo, in silico evaluation and topical gel formulation of Erythrina crista-galli L. flower ethanol extract for antibacterial, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity against acne-associated skin inflammation Short Hypothesis: A Carbopol 940-based moisturizing gel containing 1.2% (w/v) ethanol extract of Erythrina crista-galli L. flowers produces greater anti-inflammatory effect in carrageenan-induced mouse paw edema and greater in vitro inhibition of Propionibacterium acnes growth than vehicle gel, because extract bioactives (e.g., cyanidin-3-O-glucoside) bind and inhibit COX-2 and bacterial fatty acid isomerase. Related Work: Existing approaches to evaluating plant extracts for dermatological use commonly combine in vitro antioxidant assays (DPPH), in vitro antibacterial screens (disc diffusion, and sometimes broth microdilution), in vivo anti-inflammatory models (carrageenan-induced paw edema), in silico docking, and topical formulation stability testing. Limitations include: (1) reliance on disc diffusion without standardized MIC/MBC under anaerobic conditions for P. acnes, which yields low quantitative comparability; (2) frequent absence of systematic dose–response and power calculations in animal studies and limited histological end points; (3) in silico docking often reported without experimental target validation or ADMET evaluation; (4) topical formulation studies frequently lack skin penetration/permeation, full stability under accelerated conditions, and human-relevant irritation/ sensitization profiling; and (5) poor standardization and chemical characterization of plant extracts leading to reproducibility and scaling problems. Abstract: This pipeline defines an integrated experimental sequence to evaluate Erythrina crista-galli L. flower ethanol extract as a topical adjunct for acne-associated skin inflammation. The pipeline combines standardized in vitro antioxidant and antibacterial assays (quantitative DPPH and anaerobic MIC/MBC against Propionibacterium acnes), in vivo anti-inflammatory efficacy testing (carrageenan-induced paw edema with volumetry and histology), target-focused in silico docking and ADMET profiling of candidate phytochemicals, and formulation of a Carbopol 940-based moisturizing gel with systematic physical stability and irritation testing. The main contribution is a reproducible, multi-modal workflow that links chemical constituents to mechanism hypotheses (COX-2 and bacterial fatty-acid isomerase inhibition), quantifies bioactivity across assays, and produces a characterized topical prototype whose physical and safety profiles are benchmarked against vehicle and pharmacopeial controls. Expected outcomes are (i) quantitative activity metrics (IC50, MIC/MBC, edema inhibition), (ii) prioritized compound-target pairs for follow-up validation, and (iii) a physically stable, non-irritant gel formulation demonstrating enhanced biological activity compared with vehicle. Experiments: 1) Materials and samples: standardized ethanol (70%) extract of E. crista-galli L. flowers prepared by maceration with dry weight-to-solvent ratio and recorded yield; chemical profiling by HPLC-MS to quantify anthocyanins (target: cyanidin-3-O-glucoside) and total phenolics. 2) In vitro antioxidant: DPPH assay in triplicate across seven concentrations (1–1000 μg/mL); compute IC50 and Antioxidant Activity Index (AAI). Baseline: ascorbic acid. Metric: IC50 (μg/mL), AAI. 3) In vitro antibacterial: Propionibacterium acnes ATCC 11827 grown under anaerobic conditions. Perform disc diffusion (3 concentrations: 100%, 75%, 50% w/v) and broth microdilution to determine MIC and MBC (eight-step twofold dilution). Replicates: n=6 per condition. Baselines: clindamycin (1.2%), vehicle (DMSO/gel). Metrics: inhibition zone (mm), MIC (μg/mL), MBC (μg/mL). 4) In vivo anti-inflammatory efficacy: male mice randomized into groups (vehicle, positive control sodium diclofenac, extract oral doses 75, 150, 300 mg/kg, and topical gel groups with matched extract concentrations); n≥8 animals per group (power analysis target 80% at α=0.05). Induce paw edema with 1% carrageenan; measure paw volume at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120 minutes by plethysmometry; compute percent edema and percent inhibition; collect paw tissue for histology and neutrophil counts. Metrics: percent inhibition at 120 min, area under curve of edema, inflammatory cell density (cells/mm2). Statistics: two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc. 5) In silico docking and ADMET: prepare 3D structures for identified phytochemicals and target proteins (COX-2, AKR1B10, bacterial fatty-acid isomerase); energy minimize ligands; run Autodock Vina with defined grid boxes; report top binding affinities (kcal/mol), predicted binding modes, and ligand efficiency; run ADMET predictions (solubility, skin permeability, cytotoxicity). Baseline comparator ligands: diclofenac, clindamycin, vitamin C. 6) Formulation and physical testing: prepare three gel formulations (F1 no extract, F2 0.7% w/v extract, F3 1.2% w/v extract) using Carbopol 940 base; perform organoleptic, homogeneity, pH, adhesion, spreadability, viscosity (rotational viscometer), accelerated stability (3 cycles: 4°C/25°C/40°C, 72 h each), and in vivo dermal irritation (OECD-adapted, n=6). Metrics: pH range, spread diameter (cm), viscosity (cP), adhesion (s), percent change after cycles, irritation score. 7) Comparison and ablation studies: (A) compare crude extract vs HPLC-enriched fraction containing cyanidin-3-O-glucoside in antibacterial and anti-inflammatory assays; (B) compare topical gel delivery vs equivalent topical application of extract in solution (same dose) to assess formulation effect; (C) vary Carbopol concentration (1.0% vs 1.4% w/v) to test impact on bioactivity delivery and spreadability. 8) Data analysis: report means±SD, ANOVA or Kruskal–Wallis as appropriate, effect sizes, and 95% confidence intervals. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Plant material variability and extract standardization: phytochemical content may vary with harvest, causing batch-to-batch activity differences. 2) Translation limits: carrageenan paw edema is an acute inflammatory model and may not recapitulate chronic acne pathophysiology or human skin microenvironment. 3) Culture limitations: P. acnes is anaerobic; disc diffusion lacks sensitivity and may not reflect MIC under physiologic sebum conditions. 4) Bioavailability and penetration: topical gel may not deliver sufficient active compound through stratum corneum to reach follicular targets; measured in vitro activity may not translate to topical efficacy. 5) In silico limitations: docking predictions can generate false positives and do not guarantee biochemical inhibition or cellular activity. 6) Safety risks: potential for skin irritation, sensitization, or systemic toxicity at higher doses not apparent in short-term tests. 7) Statistical and scale constraints: limited sample sizes may reduce statistical power; scale-up for manufacturing may alter physicochemical properties and stability. 8) Regulatory and ethical constraints: animal model use and human application will require approvals and may limit direct clinical extrapolation.
